lesson.title: Pilot, place and test
lesson.subtitle: Test one sensor, put it in the right place, and set alerts you can trust

video.title: Pilot, place and test
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor in a hot classroom; ten small sensor boxes in a row on the windowsills, each showing a green light. Pupils in the middle rows yawn.
scenes.animation: Green lights blink one after another; a yawn spreads across the room.
scenes.narration: We built ten CO₂ sensors before testing one. All ten sat on windowsills, by open windows. They read fresh air while pupils inside yawned. Ten times the work, ten times the mistake.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: pilot one sensor, place it well, and set alerts you can trust.

scenes.visual: One sensor box on a bench with a notebook beside it; a calendar flips through two weeks; notes pile up.
scenes.animation: Calendar pages flip; ticks and crosses appear in the notebook.
scenes.narration: A pilot is one sensor node, tested before you build many. One mistake is cheap to fix; ten are not. Run it a week or two, and note everything that goes wrong.

scenes.visual: A test sheet on a clipboard with four checkboxes; a pupil holds the sensor outside in the schoolyard.
scenes.animation: Each box ticks as it is said.
scenes.narration: Write the test first. Outdoors, it should read about four hundred and twenty ppm. It should report all week, with no gaps. And it should rise as the class fills, and fall when windows open.

scenes.visual: A classroom plan from above: a green tick on the side wall at head height, red crosses by the window, the door, the fan and a sunny patch.
scenes.animation: Ticks and crosses stamp onto the plan.
scenes.narration: Place it where it measures what you mean: the air pupils breathe. That's seated head height, a metre or two from anyone. Not by windows, doors or fans, and not in the sun.

scenes.visual: Three small pictures: a tank lid with a sensor, a garden bed with a probe at root depth, a white louvred box in the shade.
scenes.animation: Each picture slides in with a tick.
scenes.narration: Each sensor has its own rule. Tank: on the lid, away from the inlet pipe. Soil: at root depth, not on the path. Thermometer: in shade, in moving air.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma at her desk, mid-sentence, with a small sensor box right beside her. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The CO₂ sensor sits on my desk, a hand's width from where I talk all day. What will it show?

scenes.visual: A puff of breath drifts onto the sensor; its number jumps. The sensor moves to the side wall and the number settles.
scenes.animation: The number spikes, then settles after the move.
scenes.narration: Higher than the room. Breath out holds about a hundred times more CO₂ than outdoor air. Keep the sensor a metre or two from people.

scenes.visual: A sensor with a traffic light on its front: green, amber, red, each with its range.
scenes.animation: The light steps from green to amber to red.
scenes.narration: Now the alert. Below eight hundred ppm, the room is well aired. From eight hundred to fifteen hundred, open a window soon. Above fifteen hundred, open them all now. Where you draw the line decides which mistakes you make.

scenes.visual: Two panels: a red light over a fresh, airy room; a green light over a stuffy room with sleepy pupils.
scenes.animation: A slider moves the line down; the false-alarm pile grows as the miss pile shrinks.
scenes.narration: Every alert makes two kinds of mistake. A false alarm: the light goes red, but the air is fine. A miss: the air is bad, with no warning. Lower the line: more false alarms, fewer misses.

scenes.visual: A balance: a dry tap on one side, a pile of ignored red lights on the other. Then a line chart from the pilot with the threshold drawn across.
scenes.animation: The balance tips each way; the line chart draws itself.
scenes.narration: So which mistake costs more? For the tank, a miss means a day without water: warn early. In a stuffy room, too many false alarms and teachers ignore the light. Test your line on the pilot's data.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph beside a phone showing a silent alert app and a water tank behind him. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The tank alert keeps going off for nothing. A colleague moves the threshold until it never does. Problem solved?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: one sensor, a clipboard, a map pin, a balance.
scenes.narration: No: an alert that never goes off misses every real problem. Find the balance on real data. Remember: pilot one, write the test, place it well, and choose the mistakes you can live with.

scenes.visual: Pupils move round the classroom with one thermometer; a table on the board fills with five readings.
scenes.animation: Readings appear in the table; one row gets a circle.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: a placement hunt. With one thermometer, pupils take readings in five places, from the window to the sunny corner. They compare, and choose the best spot with a reason. Next time: keeping it running and secure.

checkpoints.prompt: A CO₂ sensor sits on the teacher's desk, a hand's width from where she talks. What will it show?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — every breath out is rich in CO₂, so a sensor by someone's mouth reads too high.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — her breath reaches the sensor first, so it reads higher than the air pupils breathe. Keep it a metre or two from people.

checkpoints.prompt: An alert kept going off for nothing, so a colleague moved the threshold until it never goes off. Problem solved?

options.text: No — now it misses real problems

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — an alert that never goes off misses every real problem. Find the balance, and test it on real data.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with no false alarms, it now misses real problems too: the tank can run dry with no warning.
